subject: geography
topicDisplay: Geographic Themes Three From The Sl List
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does 'energy transition' typically refer to today?
options: Moving power stations to new locations
Switching homes from gas to oil
The shift from fossil fuels towards low-carbon and renewable sources
questions.explain: The contemporary energy transition is the structural move away from fossil fuels towards renewable and low-carbon energy.

questions.q: Which is an example of an unconventional fossil fuel source?
questions.explain: Shale gas, released by hydraulic fracturing, is an unconventional source requiring more advanced extraction than conventional reserves.

questions.q: Mantle convection currents are driven primarily by:
options: Heat from radioactive decay in the core and mantle
questions.explain: Heat from radioactive decay (and residual primordial heat) sets up convection cells in the mantle.

questions.q: Constructive waves are associated with:
options: Steep wave fronts and rapid cliff retreat
High frequency, strong backwash and beach erosion
Low frequency, strong swash and net deposition
questions.explain: Constructive waves have low frequency and a strong swash relative to backwash, building up the beach.

questions.q: What distinguishes physical water scarcity from economic water scarcity?
options: Economic scarcity means too little water; physical means high prices
Physical scarcity means too little water; economic scarcity means lack of investment to access available water
questions.explain: Physical scarcity is an absolute shortage of water, whereas economic scarcity is failure to access water that exists due to inadequate infrastructure or investment.

questions.q: Hydraulic action as a marine erosion process operates by:
options: The grinding of rock by sediment carried in waves
Air compressed in joints by breaking waves, weakening the rock
Rock fragments colliding and becoming rounded
The dissolving of calcium carbonate in seawater
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the force of water and trapped, compressed air shattering rock in cracks and joints.

questions.q: Which is a sub-aerial process operating on a cliff face?
questions.explain: Sub-aerial processes (weathering and mass movement, e.g. slumping) act on the land above the wave zone.

questions.q: Basaltic (mafic) lava typically produces which volcano type?
questions.explain: Low-silica basaltic lava is runny and flows far, building broad, gently-sloping shield volcanoes.

questions.q: An esker is a fluvioglacial landform consisting of:
options: An unsorted ridge of till at the glacier margin
A winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel deposited in a subglacial meltwater tunnel
A steep-sided trough eroded by ice
questions.explain: Eskers are sinuous ridges of sorted sediment laid down by meltwater streams flowing within or beneath the ice.

questions.q: As a tsunami approaches shallow coastal water it:
options: Slows down and increases dramatically in height (shoaling)
Decreases in height and increases in speed
questions.explain: In shallow water the wave slows and its energy is compressed, causing wave height to build greatly through shoaling.

questions.q: Hot spots such as Hawaii are explained by:
options: A plume of rising magma from the mantle independent of plate boundaries
questions.explain: A stationary mantle plume melts the overriding plate as it moves, producing a chain of volcanoes away from any margin.

questions.q: A terminal moraine marks:
options: The maximum extent of a glacier's advance, deposited at its snout
The lateral edge of a glacier
questions.explain: A terminal moraine is the ridge of till deposited at the furthest point a glacier reached before retreat.

questions.q: Which is a key challenge in feeding a growing global population?
options: Balancing rising demand with limited land, water and the impacts of climate change
questions.explain: Producing enough food for a growing population while constrained by finite land and water and a changing climate is a central challenge.

questions.q: Plucking as a glacial erosion process occurs when:
options: Rivers deposit sediment beneath the glacier
Meltwater refreezes onto bedrock and pulls fragments away as the ice moves
Rock debris embedded in ice scratches and grinds the bedrock
Frost shatters exposed rock above the ice
questions.explain: Plucking happens when meltwater freezes onto rock, and the moving ice tears loose blocks of bedrock.

questions.q: A spit forms where:
options: Two headlands erode into a single bay
Wave refraction concentrates energy on a headland
Longshore drift extends a ridge of deposited material across a bay or estuary
A river deposits a delta offshore
questions.explain: Spits develop where longshore drift carries sediment beyond a change in coastline orientation and deposits it.

questions.q: Longshore drift transports sediment along a coast because:
options: Backwash carries material directly back up the beach
Waves always approach perpendicular to the shore
Swash approaches at an angle while backwash returns straight down the slope
Tidal currents move sediment offshore only
questions.explain: Angled swash and gravity-driven perpendicular backwash move material in a zig-zag along the beach.

questions.q: In the Park (hazard-response) model, the curve plots quality of life or economic activity against:
options: Time, through pre-disaster, disruption, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction phases
questions.explain: Park's model shows quality of life over time across stages from relief through rehabilitation to reconstruction.

questions.q: Conservative (transform) margins produce earthquakes but no volcanoes because:
options: Magma is too viscous to erupt
Plates move apart, allowing magma up
Plates slide past one another, so no crust is created or destroyed
questions.explain: At conservative margins plates move laterally past each other; crust is neither created nor subducted, so there is friction-driven seismicity but no magma generation.

questions.q: What is the main aim of 'resource stewardship'?
options: Managing resources sustainably to balance present needs with future availability
questions.explain: Resource stewardship promotes sustainable management so resources remain available for future generations.

questions.q: S-waves cannot travel through the outer core, which is evidence that the outer core is:
questions.explain: S-waves cannot pass through liquids; their absence beyond the core-mantle boundary indicates a liquid outer core.

questions.q: Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) is distinctive because it:
options: Manages only a single town's seafront in isolation
Takes a holistic, long-term view of the whole coastal zone and its stakeholders
questions.explain: ICZM coordinates management across the entire coastal zone, balancing economic, social and environmental needs.

questions.q: Which best describes the geopolitics of energy?
options: Control of energy supplies and pathways becomes a source of power and conflict between states
questions.explain: Because energy is unevenly distributed, controlling reserves and supply routes confers political leverage and can drive tension.

questions.q: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by:
options: Vertical displacement of the sea floor during a submarine earthquake
questions.explain: Sudden vertical movement of the sea floor, typically at subduction zones, displaces the water column and generates a tsunami.

questions.q: A nuee ardente (pyroclastic flow), as at Montserrat, is a secondary volcanic hazard consisting of:
options: A fast, hot mixture of gas, ash and rock fragments flowing downslope
questions.explain: Pyroclastic flows are superheated, ground-hugging avalanches of gas, ash and volcanic debris that move at lethal speed.

questions.q: Why can large dam projects create both benefits and conflicts?
options: They provide power and water storage but can displace people and reduce downstream flow
questions.explain: Dams deliver hydropower and storage yet can flood communities, alter ecosystems and reduce water reaching downstream users.

questions.q: The periglacial process of frost heave produces:
options: Patterned ground through repeated freeze-thaw sorting of material
questions.explain: Frost heave repeatedly lifts and sorts stones, generating patterned ground in periglacial environments.

questions.q: Resilience to tectonic hazards is best described as the ability of a community to:
options: Absorb, adapt to and recover from a hazard event
Predict the exact time of every earthquake
questions.explain: Resilience is the capacity to withstand, adapt to and bounce back from a hazard impact.

questions.q: Why is food security about more than just total production?
options: It also requires availability, access, utilisation and stability of supply
questions.explain: Food security needs adequate availability, physical and economic access, proper nutrition and stable supply over time.

questions.q: The moment magnitude scale (Mw) is logarithmic; an increase of one whole unit represents roughly how much more energy released?
questions.explain: Each whole step on the magnitude scale corresponds to about a 32-fold increase in energy released.

questions.q: What does 'peak oil' refer to?
options: The point at which global oil production reaches its maximum before declining
The highest oil price ever recorded
questions.explain: Peak oil is the hypothesised point of maximum global production, after which output is expected to fall.
